summary: Defines MIB objects for managing RIP version 2 with SNMP. It is a standards-track document that gives network management tools a standard view of RIP-2 routers.

plainLanguage.summary: This document gives network managers a standard way to see and control RIP on a router using SNMP. It defines counters for route changes and queries, a table of per-interface statistics, a table that says which version of RIP each interface sends and accepts, what authentication it uses and what metric it advertises, and an optional table listing the neighbouring routers it has heard from.

questions: what is the rip version 2 mib
how to manage rip with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a manager see and steer a router's RIP-2 interfaces, and watch its neighbours.

tldr.problem: A network manager needs to see what RIP is doing on a router: which interfaces it is running on, which version it is speaking, how many updates it has sent, and who its neighbours are.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a MIB module with a set of global counters, a statistics table and a configuration table indexed by interface address, and an optional table of peers. Configuration objects control the RIP version sent and accepted, the authentication type and key, the default metric and the source address.
tldr.outcome: The module is registered at { mib-2 23 }. It deprecates the route domain objects that RFC 1389 defined, adds support for unnumbered interfaces through a pseudo-address, and adds the two Demand RIP settings that otherwise would have needed a separate MIB.

today: RFC 1724 is a Draft Standard from November 1994 and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 1389 with a version that drops the deprecated route domain objects, handles unnumbered interfaces, and covers the two Demand RIP settings that would otherwise have needed a MIB of their own.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework has three components. The SMI, in STD 16, defines the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. STD 16 defines a more concise description mechanism that is wholly consistent with the SMI. RFC 1156 defines MIB-I, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols, and STD 17 defines MIB-II, an evolution of MIB-I based on implementation experience and new operational requirements. The SNMP, in STD 15, is the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and are defined using the subset of ASN.1 defined in the SMI. Each object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name that specifies an object type; the object type together with an object instance identifies one instantiation of the object. For human convenience a textual string, the OBJECT DESCRIPTOR, is often used as well. The syntax defines the abstract data structure for the object type, and the encoding is how that structure is represented, which is also how it is transmitted on the network. The SMI restricts the ASN.1 constructs that may be used, explicitly for simplicity.

Section 4 of the document contains the specification of all the object types, written with the conventions of the SMI as amended by an earlier extension. The module introduces one new data type as a textual convention, RouteTag, which represents the contents of the route domain field in the packet header or route entry. The textual conventions are an artifact of the explanatory method used: they change neither the syntax nor the semantics of any managed object, and an object defined in terms of one is still encoded by the rules that define the primitive type.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is the protocol a manager uses to read and change values on a device, and the MIB is the catalogue that names those values. Each object has a name, a type and a way of encoding it. This document adds a catalogue for RIP: counters, per-interface statistics, per-interface configuration and neighbours.

sections.title: Structure of the RIP-2 MIB
sections.content:
The RIP-2 MIB contains global counters, which are useful for detecting the deleterious effects of RIP incompatibilities; two interface tables, which hold interface-specific statistics and configuration information; and an optional peer table, containing information that may help in debugging neighbour relationships. Like the protocol itself, the MIB takes great care to preserve compatibility with RIP-1 systems and to control the monitoring and controlling of system interactions.

The global group holds two counters, the number of route changes made to the IP route database by RIP, which does not include the ageing of a route, and the number of responses sent to RIP queries from other systems. Implementing this group is mandatory for systems that implement RIP-2. The counters are meant to help when routes are changing quickly or when a neighbour is failing.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has four parts. Two global counters say how much RIP is doing. Two interface tables, one for statistics and one for configuration, say what RIP is doing on each interface. An optional peer table lists the neighbouring routers that have been heard from, which is mostly useful when something is going wrong.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 1389
sections.content:
The RIP-2 MIB was originally published in RFC 1389. It encoded the concept of a routing domain and did not address unnumbered interfaces. In the current version of the protocol, route domains are deprecated, and so they are deprecated in the MIB as well: the object rip2IfConfDomain is deprecated, and the object rip2PeerDomain, which cannot be deprecated because it is an instance object, must always be zero.

Unnumbered interfaces are supported in this version. Because the IP address that the neighbour uses may be unknown to the system, a pseudo-address identifies these interfaces: the pseudo-address is in the class A network 0.0.0.0, and the host number, the least significant 24 bits of the address, is the ifIndex value of the relevant IP interface. This is an additional new meaning for the objects rip2IfStatAddress and rip2IfConfAddress, and it is backward compatible with the RFC 1389 usage.

The object rip2IfConfSrcAddress is added, so that the source address on an unnumbered interface can be configured, and the meaning of rip2PeerAddress is broadened so that it stays relevant on unnumbered interfaces. The object rip2IfConfSend is augmented with two values for the use of Demand RIP under RIP-I and RIP-II rules, which avoids the necessity of a separate Demand RIP MIB. MD5 authentication is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of this MIB was tied to an idea the protocol has since dropped, the routing domain, so those objects are now deprecated and always zero. The new version handles interfaces that have no address of their own by using a made-up address whose last part is the interface number, and it adds a way to set the source address on such an interface, plus the two settings for Demand RIP.

sections.title: The Objects: Counters, Interfaces and Peers
sections.content:
The statistics table holds one row per interface that runs RIP, indexed by the interface address. Its counters are the number of RIP response packets received and then discarded for any reason, such as a version 0 packet or an unknown command type; the number of routes in otherwise valid RIP packets that were ignored, for example because of an unknown address family or an invalid metric; and the number of triggered RIP updates actually sent on the interface, which explicitly does not include full updates sent with new information. The row status object is read-create, and writing invalid to it deletes the interface.

The configuration table holds one row per subnet that needs separate RIP configuration, and it is where a manager steers the protocol. rip2IfConfAuthType chooses the authentication used on the interface: no authentication, a simple password or MD5. rip2IfConfAuthKey holds the key itself, up to 16 octets; a shorter value is left-justified and padded on the right with nulls, and reading the object always returns a zero-length string, so that authentication cannot be bypassed by reading the key out of the MIB. rip2IfConfSend says what the router sends on the interface: nothing, RIP-1 updates compliant with RFC 1058, RIP-2 updates broadcast using the RFC 1058 route subsumption rules, RIP-2 updates multicast, or Demand RIP on a WAN interface under version 1 or version 2 rules. rip2IfConfReceive says which versions are accepted. rip2IfConfDefaultMetric is the metric used for the default route advertised on the interface, and a value of zero means no default route is originated. rip2IfConfSrcAddress is the source address the system uses on the interface, which on a numbered interface must be the same as the interface address, and on an unnumbered interface must be the address of some interface on the system.

The optional peer table holds one row per routing peer, indexed by the peer address and the peer domain. It reports the source address the peer is using, the value of the routing domain field in the packets received from it, which must now be zero, the value of sysUpTime when the most recent RIP update was received from that peer, the RIP version number in the header of the last packet received, and the number of response packets from that peer discarded as invalid. An active peer is a router from which a valid RIP update has been heard in the last 180 seconds. The module's conformance statement lists the global, interface statistics, interface configuration and peer groups as mandatory groups, even though the peer group is described as optional to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: The statistics table counts the bad packets and the triggered updates per interface. The configuration table is where the manager decides what each interface sends and accepts, which authentication it uses and what metric it advertises by default. The peer table records the neighbours, when each was last heard from and which RIP version they speak. The authentication key can be set but never read back, so a manager cannot learn it by asking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document is brief on this point: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The relevant material is therefore in the RIP-2 protocol specification itself, and in the MIB definitions, where the authentication key is the one object that is treated carefully: reading it always returns an empty string, and a modification of the authentication type does not modify the key that is stored.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says nothing about security. The one thing it does do is make sure the authentication key cannot be read back out of the MIB, and that changing the authentication type does not change the key.

viz.caption: WHERE THE OBJECTS SIT IN THE MIB TREE

items.title: rip2Globals
items.text: Route changes made by RIP and the number of responses sent to RIP queries.

items.title: rip2IfStatTable
items.text: Per-interface counters: bad packets received, bad routes ignored and triggered updates sent.

items.title: rip2IfConfTable
items.text: Per-interface configuration: version sent and accepted, authentication, default metric and source address.

items.title: rip2PeerTable
items.text: Optional. The neighbours, the last update from each, and the RIP version they speak.

viz.caption: THE CONFIGURATION VALUES FOR A RIP INTERFACE

items.label: rip2IfConfSend
items.desc: doNotSend: send nothing on this interface.

items.label: rip2IfConfSend
items.desc: ripVersion1: send RIP updates compliant with RFC 1058.

items.label: rip2IfConfSend
items.desc: rip1Compatible: broadcast RIP-2 updates using RFC 1058 route subsumption rules.

items.label: rip2IfConfSend
items.desc: ripV1Demand: use Demand RIP on a WAN interface under version 1 rules.

items.label: rip2IfConfSend
items.desc: ripV2Demand: use Demand RIP on a WAN interface under version 2 rules.

items.label: rip2IfConfReceive
items.desc: rip2: accept version 2 updates, including multicast packets.

items.label: rip2IfConfReceive
items.desc: rip1OrRip2: accept either, including multicast packets.

viz.caption: THE COLUMNS OF A CONFIGURATION ROW, VERBATIM FROM SECTION 4

data.title: Rip2IfConfEntry
data.code:
Rip2IfConfEntry ::= SEQUENCE {
    rip2IfConfAddress        IpAddress,
    rip2IfConfDomain         RouteTag,
    rip2IfConfAuthType       INTEGER,
    rip2IfConfAuthKey        OCTET STRING (SIZE(0..16)),
    rip2IfConfSend           INTEGER,
    rip2IfConfReceive        INTEGER,
    rip2IfConfDefaultMetric  INTEGER,
    rip2IfConfStatus         RowStatus,
    rip2IfConfSrcAddress     IpAddress
}
